stem: When should you dim your high beams?
choices: Within 200 feet of an oncoming vehicle
Only when the other driver flashes their lights
Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle, and when following a vehicle within 500 feet
explanation:
**Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle** and **when following another vehicle within 500 feet.** Use high beams when it is safe and legal.

**Wrong choices**
- Within 200 feet of an oncoming vehicle: 200 feet is too late. The other driver is already blinded.
- Only when the other driver flashes their lights: You must dim even if they do not flash.

stem: If you must drive in fog, which lights should you use?
choices: Low-beam headlights and fog lights
High-beam headlights
Parking lights only
oneLineConcept: Fog: low beams and fog lights
explanation:
The best advice for fog is to **pull off and wait**. If you must drive, **slow down before you enter the fog**, use **low beams and fog lights** even in daytime, turn on your four-way flashers, and avoid passing.

**Wrong choices**
- High-beam headlights: High beams reflect off the fog and make it harder to see.
- Parking lights only: Parking lights make you hard for others to see.

stem: On a very hot day, your tire pressure reads higher than normal. What should you do?
choices: Let some air out to bring it back to normal
Do not let air out. The pressure will drop when the tire cools.
Drive faster so air flow cools the tires
oneLineConcept: Never let air out of hot tires
explanation:
Air pressure **rises with temperature**. **Do not let air out**, or the pressure will be too low when the tire cools. If a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools, or it may blow out or catch fire.

**Wrong choices**
- Let some air out to bring it back to normal: Then the tire will be under-inflated once it cools.
- Drive faster so air flow cools the tires: Higher speed makes tires hotter.

stem: When is it safe to remove the radiator cap?
choices: Any time the engine is not overheated
Any time, as long as you wear gloves
Only after the cooling system has cooled down
oneLineConcept: Open the radiator cap only when cool
explanation:
**Never remove the radiator cap until the system has cooled.** Steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns. If you can touch the cap with your bare hand, it is probably cool enough.

**Wrong choices**
- Any time the engine is not overheated: A hot system is under pressure even if it is not overheating.
- Any time, as long as you wear gloves: Gloves do not protect you from a spray of boiling coolant.

choices: A thin layer of clear ice that makes the road look only wet
Thick, dark ice that is easy to see
Ice that forms only on gravel roads
oneLineConcept: Black ice looks like a wet road
explanation:
**Black ice is a thin layer clear enough to see the road through.** It makes the road **look wet**. Any time the temperature is below freezing and the road looks wet, watch out for black ice.

**Wrong choices**
- Thick, dark ice that is easy to see: Black ice is hard to see. That is why it is dangerous.
- Ice that forms only on gravel roads: It can form on any road surface.

stem: You have just driven through deep standing water. What should you do with your brakes?
choices: Brake as hard as you can right away to test them
Keep light pressure on the brakes for a short distance to dry them, then make a test stop
Nothing. Brakes dry out on their own in seconds
oneLineConcept: Wet brakes: light pressure, then test stop
explanation:
Water can make brakes weak, uneven, or grabby. After going through water:

1. **Keep light pressure on the brakes for a short distance** to heat and dry them.
2. **Make a test stop** when it is safe (check that no one is behind you).
3. If they still do not work well, dry them more the same way.

**Wrong choices**
- Brake as hard as you can right away to test them: Hard braking with wet brakes can cause lockups or pulling.
- Nothing. Brakes dry out on their own in seconds: Wet brakes can be weak or grab. You need to dry them.

stem: In very hot weather, how often should you inspect your tires?
choices: Every 4 hours or every 200 miles
Only at the end of the day
Every 2 hours or every 100 miles
oneLineConcept: Hot weather: tires every 2 hours or 100 miles
explanation:
Heat raises tire pressure and the risk of blowouts and fires. **In very hot weather, inspect the tires every two hours or every 100 miles.**

**Wrong choices**
- Every 4 hours or every 200 miles: This is too long between checks in very hot weather.
- Only at the end of the day: Heat can damage tires during the trip.
